results.title: DeKalb County Sanitation Division – Employee Hip-Hop Competition (Round 1)
results.creator: DCTV
results.description: Produced by DCTV (DeKalb County Television) Channel 23, this video presents round one of the Employee Hip-Hop Competition to help spread the word about the Sanitation Division’s one-day-a-week collection service change program themed, “Rolling Forward to One – DeKalb’s Approach to Recycling & Solid Waste Management.” Additional Information: In this first-ever, DeKalb hip-hop competition, employees from various county departments and divisions vie for an opportunity to record a track for the county’s official “Rolling Forward to One” public service announcement. Contestants rap about the benefits and highlights of the new sanitation collection service change, as well as the benefits of recycling. Judges represent various county departments and divisions as well. Auditions for round one were held May 8, 2015. The finals will be held May 15, 2015. The event is being covered by DCTV, and CBS Radio’s V-103 Radio DJ, Greg Street, served as the master of ceremonies. Contestants Yashetrius Anderson – 311 Citizen Help Center Janet Barksdale – Planning & Sustainability Veronica Daniels – Sanitation Division Joseph Ellison – Fire Rescue Victor Hill – Finance Stanley Patrick – Tax Commissioner’s Office Angela Smith – Property Appraisal (via recorded video) Richard Smith – Library Judges Charles L. Mason III – Assistant Director, Public Works Diamond Lewis Miller – Director, DeKalb County Television (DCTV) Alison Weissinger – Director, Library Chris Morris – Former Director, Community Development Gordon Burkette – Program Manager, Keep DeKalb Beautiful (KDB) Captain Eric Jackson – Public Information Officer, Fire Rescue James Breedlove – Production Assistant, DeKalb County Television (DCTV) Michael Johnson (Mixzo) - Music Producer If you’d like to find out more about DeKalb’s Sanitation Division, call (404) 294-2900 or go to the County’s webpage at DeKalbCountyGA.Gov, and look for the Sanitation Division. For more information about DeKalb County, visit http://www.DeKalbCountyGA.gov. And, for the latest on DeKalb County news, visit http://www.dctvchannel23.tv.

results.title: Bozeman City Commission Meeting - October 6, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # Bozeman City Commission Regular Meeting – October 6, 2026 The Bozeman City Commission met on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at 6:00 PM in the Commission Room at City Hall. The meeting included consent agenda approvals, public testimony on a proposed parking district, a mayoral proclamation for Fire Prevention Week, a special presentation on the 70th Montana Legislature, and a work session on potential community ballot issues. No final decisions were made on ballot measures, but commissioners narrowed focus to housing and transit funding for the near term. ### Consent Calendar - **F.2**: Ratified a Montana Department of Transportation grant to fund a full-time traffic enforcement officer in the Bozeman Police Department. - **F.3** was pulled from the agenda. - All remaining consent items (F.1, F.4–F.11) were approved unanimously (5–0). ### Public Comments & Testimony - **Gallatin High School Parking District**: Multiple residents (Courtney Johnson, Richard Smith, Joshua Stack, Kim Falls, Ron Salto, Scott Johnson, Brianne Walsh, and others) expressed strong support for advancing a residential parking permit district near Gallatin High School. They cited safety hazards, obstructed sightlines, and near-miss accidents involving pedestrians and cyclists. Speakers urged the Commission to schedule a hearing—possibly by a special meeting—before further delay. Several noted the process has stretched into its third year despite unanimous Transportation Advisory Board recommendation. A second-grade child (Audrey) also testified about feeling unsafe while biking. - **Non‑agenda comments**: - Janae Johnson (CEO, Bozeman Public Library Friends and Foundation) announced a private‑funded West Side Library Branch (estimated $25–$30 million) to be gifted to the city, with a request for an operating levy in 2029. - Mark Campanelli (Bogert Park Neighbors Association) expressed frustration with parking enforcement and neighborhood responsiveness, cautioning against labeling residents as NIMBYs. ### Mayoral Proclamation - Mayor Morrison proclaimed October 4–10, 2026 as **Fire Prevention Week** with the theme “Charge into Safety – Safe Charging is a Superpower,” emphasizing safe use of lithium‑ion batteries. ### Special Presentation: 70th Session of the Montana Legislature - Staff (Jesse DiTommaso, Economic Development Coordinator) and lobbyist Danny Hess (Central House Strategies) outlined the city’s legislative preparation. Key points: - Nearly 700 bill draft requests already filed. - Priority system for city staff review: highest impact on current operations, then adopted city plans, then beneficial bills. - Proactive efforts include a municipal water bill linking land‑use planning with water planning, in partnership with other cities and the League of Cities and Towns. - Monitoring property tax reform, local government interim committee studies (special districts, voted bonds/levies), and water policy (exempt wells). - Discussion of a potential local voter‑approved tourist tax to generate revenue for city services. ### Work Session: Community Ballot Issues Commissioners discussed possible ballot measures for 2027–2028, guided by a rubric evaluating urgency, cost, community support, and scope. No binding decisions were made, but consensus emerged on several points: #### Priority Areas - **Housing**: Identified as the top priority. Commissioners expressed support for a dedicated funding source (e.g., a property tax levy or bond) to address gaps in deeply affordable rental and entry‑level homeownership. The city has 10 acres of land (Fowler site + five acres from Turnrow annexation) that could be used for mixed‑income development. A levy failure in 2021 was attributed to lack of specific spending plan. - **Streamline Transit (GVUTD)**: The Urban Transportation District is considering a funding measure in fall 2027 or spring 2028. Commissioners noted strong past voter support (79% approved district creation) and the importance of transit as the second largest household expense ($13,000/year on average). Streamline provided 165,000 rides in the prior year. - **Fire Station #4**: Discussed as a high‑cost, city‑only need, but commissioners expressed caution after a recent ballot failure. City Manager noted a SAFER grant funds 12 firefighters for two years; ongoing operations would require voter‑approved levy or bond. - **Pool, Library, Senior Center, Mental/Behavioral Health, EMS**: These were considered longer‑term or regional issues. The library foundation will seek an operating levy no earlier than 2029. EMS and behavioral health may require county‑wide or special district solutions (possible 2028 ballot). The senior center has $1.4 million in CIP improvements but no ballot ask scheduled. #### Next Steps - Commissioners agreed to fund a statistically valid survey (budgeted) to test voter support for housing and transit levies, and potentially other items like aquatics and fire station. - City Manager directed to develop a survey scope and timeline, with results expected before December 1, 2026. - Staff will present detailed housing plans at a November 10 work session (Fowler consensus process) and December 1 work session (municipal revenue bonds). - The Gallatin High School parking district hearing remains scheduled for December 1; City Manager offered to explore moving it sooner. ### Key Outcomes - **Consent agenda approved** (items F.1, F.2, F.4–F.11) 5–0. - **No formal votes** on ballot issues; direction given to staff to prepare polling and refine housing proposals. - Parking district hearing currently set for December 1, 2026; City Manager will investigate accelerating the date. - Future work sessions will further define housing funding mechanisms and transit levy options.

results.title: The Sea-Gull Cry
results.creator: Nathan, Robert, 1894-
results.description: "It’s post World War II, and nineteen-year-old LOUISA and her younger brother JERI have fled from Eastern Europe after their parents were killed. They now live in an old boat, beached on Cape Cod, thanks to the generosity of a local couple, the BAGHOTS. A frustrated local college professor RICHARD SMITH purchases a boat to escape his lonely and unfulfilled life. He, instead, crashes it onto the beach not far from Louisa and Jeri. Romantic feelings between Richard and Louisa begin to develop even though neither one thinks the other is interested. Meanwhile, Jeri begins a tentative romance with MEGAN, the niece of the Baghots. Robert Nathan crafts a tender and touching tale of the rapture and innocence that come with the discovery of first love." Review at Google newspaper archives: " that strange and beautiful story of young refugees on Cape Cod ." Digitized by google.

results.description: Declassified and Approved ForRelease2013/08/16 : CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 411 I P8 DRAFT TECHNICAL PROPOSAL ENGINEERING SUPPORT TO THE PRINTING AND PHOTOGRAPHY GROUP FOR MODERNIZING THE ELECTRONIC TEXT EDITING AND COMPOSITION SYSTEM JULY 1989 DISCLOSURE OF INFORMATION All information contained in this proposal is company confidential, is proprietary and has commercial and/or financial value. It has not been publicly disclosed and is not to be disclosed to any person other than an officer or employee of the U.S. Federal Government or the organization to which this proposal is addressed. Other disclosure of any information contained in this proposal must be requested by written notice to The MITRE Corporation. The MITRE Corporation Washington C3I Division 7525 Colshire Drive, McLean, Virginia 22102-3481 DRAFT Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 111 IIIP SECTION 1 TECHNICAL PROPOSAL FOR MODERNIZING THE PRINTING AND PHOTOGRAPHY GROUP ETECS OPERATION 1 INTRODUCTION This technical proposal outlines the Electronic Text Editing and Composition (ETECS) services that are currently provided by the Printing and Photography Group (P&PG) to its customers. The hardware and software systems in place within ETECS used to produce P&PG published products are described. Secondly, a view of the origin, charter, and role of the MITRE Corporation as a Federally Funded Research. and Development, Center (FFRDC) is outlined. To provide a more detailed view of MITRE as a resource to assist PUG in their ETECS modernization planning, this proposal includes a list of MITRE projects that are in place now or have been completed in , support of Agency components. Thirdly, the proposal outlines a work plan which, if adopted by P&PG, will modernize ETECS capabilities and will satisfy expressed needs of P&PG customers. The work plan is based on preliminary discussions with and information provided by P&PG Pre-press staff. These discussions focused on ETECS configuration limitations, constraints, and known requirements for system improvements. Additional requirements were identified via a survey conducted by P&PG staff. The survey was completed in response to a P&PG Management by Objectives (MBO) task, and requirements were documented in accordance with Milestone 2 of the ETECS Electronic Communications Architecture and Network MBO statement. Finally, work performed by MITRE on related Agency projects contributed to the understanding of the P&PG workflow. 1.1 BACKGROUND - ETECS The ETECS system, as currently configured, provides composition, page makeup, and typeset formatting of documents submitted by customers to P&PG. These documents may be originated by intelligence analysts or other customers using a variety of customer-owned input devices, methods and media. When the original text has been completed by the analyst and has been approved for publication, it is submitted to ETECS for page makeup and composition. This operation is commonly referred to as "front-ending" or 1-1 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 1111 411 as the "front end" to the printing operation.. Equipment used to support the front-ending operation is the. ATEX system, a PDP-11/34 processor with up to 16 display stations attached per processor: At present, there are four separate ATEX systems, each configured to operate in connection with specific input devices or information transmission media. The following section describes the ETECS workflow and the specific equipment configuration installed within the Center to compose and typeset documents and publications. 1.1.1 ETECS - Headquarters (Room G356) For Wang-originated documents prepared by intelligence analysts or other P&PG customers, original text may be submitted to ETECS via Wang formatted diskettes. These diskettes are forwarded to the ETECS Center by the customer and are processed by a Wang system installed in.P&PG facilities located in Room,GJ56. The Wang system in GJ56 has an electronic interface for information transfer from the Wang' to the ATEX 2 system. As an alternative to customer-originated text submitted to ETECS via Wang formatted diskette, text may be created .on customer-owned Wang systems, transmitted electronically to the Wang system installed in the ETECS facility and then transferred to the ATEX 2 system for composition and formatting for the typesetting equipment. As an alternative to the Wang-to-Wang text exchange, text may be submitted electronically from customer-originated Wang Alliance systems to the OIT VM host processor and from the VM host to the ATEX .3 system. Some customers originate text using microcomputers (other than Wang) and popular word processing software such as Microsoft Word, Wordperfect, Wordstar, or other customer-licensed systems. Like the,Wang, these systems may generate text on floppy diskettes for submission to ETECS'. Text input recorded on diskette by the microcomputer is converted at the ETECS center using a Shaftstall media conversion system. The Shaftstall strips off all formatting codes contained on the input medium, and produces a file readable by the ATEX 1 system. When the ETECS composition and typeset formatting input step has been completed, the output step of the Pre-press operation (input to the printing operation) is completed using Page Image Processing (PIP) equipment. Several models are available; outputs can be produced in various forms, e.g., resin coated (RC) high quality film, 70 millimeter film, or plain paper. 1.1.2 ETECS - P&PG Main Plant Within the P&PG main plant facility, ATEX equipment similar to that located in GJ56 may be used to compose and format textual information. 1,2 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 111 Should the document contain both text and graphics, XYVISION equipment is used to compose this type of document. At the main plant, text information may be input to the ATEX 0 system via an Optical Character Reader (OCR). In addition, graphics information may be input via a graphics scanner to XYVISION composition equipment. At this location, both the ATEX and XYVISION composition and typeset formatting equipment are interfaced to PIP equipment similar to that available in GJ56 at Headquarters. A XITRON switching device is used to direct output from the ATEX equipment to the appropriate page image processor for the type of output required. 1.2 BACKGROUND - THE MITRE CORPORATION This section provides information that describes the origin, charter, and role of the MITRE Corporation as a resource serving government agencies. In addition to this general information describing the MITRE Corporation, selected projects completed by MITRE technical staff in support of Agency sponsors are described.' MITRE was created in 1958 as a not-for-profit corporation chartered in the public interest. Since 1958, MITRE has served the public interest as a planning, .engineering, and advisory resource to its sponsors. MITRE is neither a part of industry nor a part of government; it operates as a link between these two entities. As a not-for-profit corporation, MITRE supports Defense and Intelligence communities and government agencies at the federal, state and local levels. MITRE plays a special role in supporting computer systems acquisitions. Manufacture of hardware and software for Sale is prohibited by charter; MITRE therefore is free from potential conflicts of interest that otherwise might arise from privileged access to sensitive or proprietary information. 1.3 MITRE SUPPORT TO AGENCY SPONSORS MITRE is currently providing systems engineering and technical support to the Agency on a variety of projects, and has a cadre of systems engineers that are badged and are familiar with Agency computer-based systems. MITRE technical staff are supporting Agency efforts including strategic planning, workstation architectures, applications for intelligence analysts, database design, network management, computer systems relocation, and security standards. Selected Agency projects are described below. 1-3 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 11111 ? The Office of Current Production and Analytic Support (CPAS) For CPAS, MITRE has recently completed the design and implementation of a demonstration system for dissemination of intelligence information in softcopy form. The system, referred to as EDS, is designed to demonstrate the feasibility of producing and disseminating intelligence information products to. consumers The demonstration system employs a multimedia approach; information can be displayed as combinations of text, graphics, cartographics, images, voice and motion video.' EDS has been implemented using a SUN Microsystems workstation and has been demonstrated to the intelligence community to Assess EDS concepts and to solicit comments and suggestions regarding the EDS demonstration implementation. ? Directorate for Science and Technology (DS&T) MITRE provides both strategic and near-term ADP planning support to the Directorate of Science and Technology (DS&T). Strategic ADP planning support is being provided to NPIC, the Office of Research and Development (ORD) and to the front office of DS&T. National Photographic and Interpretation Center (NPIC) NPIC is upgrading the computing and communications facilities of the NPIC Data System (NDS). MITRE is involved in the preparation of the RFP for the upgrade. In addition, MITRE is providing support for various aspects of imagery exploitation, including the evaluation of work in the research and development community, the specification of requirements for a softcopy workstation evolution capability and the study of the capabilities of various exploitation management systems. ? The Office of Imagery Analysis (OIA) OIA is currently expanding the capabilities of its network of workstations to enhance processing facilities such as word processing, spreadsheets, desktop publishing, and image processing. Plans are underway to improve access to community information systems such as CAMS and NDS, and to other information systems at Headquarters such as SAFE and VM. MITRE is the systems engineer for defining the OIA architecture, and to assist with the system, acquisition and installation process. 1-4 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 ? The Office of Global Issues (OGI) For OGI, MITRE is providing engineering support toward the design and development of a Narcotics Analysis Database. The database will be used for tracking and analyzing linkages among traffickers, organizations and governments. The database will provide data storage and retrieval capabilities on individuals, groups and organizations involved in drug trafficking and by automating the analysis of linkages among individuals and organizations in a manner that will support intelligence requirements. MITRE will perform the requirements analysis, the preliminary design work, and the system sizing to produce a Request for Proposal. The MITRE products will include a conceptual database model, a high level functional requirements description, and a Statement of Work (SOW) to be used in the competitive procurement of the system. ? Office of Leadership Analysis (LDA) MITRE is providing support to LDA which involves design of an interactive system (DOSSIER) for storing and retrieving biographical textual intelligence information and indexes to pictorial data. DOSSIER support includes concept of operations, functional requirements, database design, and user interface. ? The Office of Information Technology (OIT) MITRE is providing systems engineering and technical support to OIT. The support involves planning and assisting the New Building Program Office in the relocation of Agency computing facilities from five centers to two new computing centers. In addition, MITRE recently completed a project to review existing and planned OIT network management capabilities and customer service procedures. Major objectives of the study were to identify any weaknesses and deficiencies in network capabilities and procedures, and to make recommendations for improvements. To complete these objectives, MITRE interviewed key staff within OIT engineering, operations, and customer service organizations. In addition, interviews were conducted with Office of Communications (OC) staff and with supporting contractors. ? Office of Security (OS) For OS, MITRE is developing an Information Security strategic five-year plan. Tasks include a review of current information security 1-5 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 activities and a review of security requirements. In addition, key Agency staff were interviewed to define security issues and to develop a set of strategic goals and objectives to serve as a basis for the plan. The plan will describe security initiatives, and programs, resource requirements, and a schedule for implementation. 1.2.2 MITRE Facilities The MITRE Corporation has established sponsor-accredited Sensitive Compartmented Information Facilities (SCIFs) with offices and laboratory space available at both McLean, Virginia and Bedford, Massachusetts. In addition, the Corporation has offices located in an accredited SCIF in Rosslyn, Virginia. Approved information-handling systems are currently available at each of these locations for the preparation and secure storage of project documentation. 1-6 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 Declassified and Approved For Release 2013/08/16: CIA-RDP12-00036R000100160012-1 SECTION 2 2 ETECS PROBLEM STATEMENT This section identifies constraints and limitations of the ETECS equipment currently in operation within P&PG. On the basis of discussions with P&PG staff, review of MBO milestone 2 - (Determine future requirements by meeting with customers and determining their plans regarding electronic document production), contacts with other P&PG customers, together with familiarity with other Agency office requirements for printing and publishing, PUG services and facilities are deficient in the following 4k-em 1. ETECS provides a one-way electroni6tterface for transfer of information between customer-owned workstations and the ETECS facility. This one-way information flow limits the extent to which documents can be created, edited and proofed in soft-copy form. The schedule for publication turnaround is severely constrained by this limitation. The production cycle for initial and interim proofing is too long and needs to be shortened. 2. Documents are created by customers using a variety of workstations and word processing software products. The information is downloaded to the ATEX equipment, composed and typeset in a format specific to the ATEX equipment. The composed database is stored on the ATEX system, and should the originator want a copy of the database, it is returned in ASCII format on magnetic media. The database cannot be transformed easily from magnetic tape to workstation for subsequent access by the originator. A capability to return databases to customers in uncomposed format is needed. a4A dbieheel 3. The current ATEX display station is a single purpose device, and is attached to the ATEX PDP-11/34 system for text composition and page layout operation only. The display station is a "dumb" video display without many of the features common to other multi-purpose PC-based workstations. results.title: Donald Hartung Trial - Defense Opening Statement
results.creator: Law&Crime Network
results.description: NOTE: This is a Death Penalty Case. Donald Hartung, 63, stands trial in Escambia County, Florida for allegedly killing his mother Voncile Smith, 77, and his half-brothers John William Smith, 49, and Richard Thomas Smith, 47. He faces three counts of first-degree premeditated murder. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Escambia County deputies say the crimes happened July 28, 2015, according to an amended arrest report obtained by Law&Crime. Richard Smith, an employee of the Department of Homeland Security, had no-showed worked for a few days, so on deputies checked up on him on July 31. They found no sign of forced entry, but were able to enter through the back with the help of firefighters, and found the three victims dead throughout the home. Each person was under “large piles of clothes,” deputies said. Richard Smith had been shot around his right ear, and had a stab wound to the throat, deputies said. He was found face down in the TV room at the foot of the TV, investigators said. Authorities said he was wearing the same clothes he’d been wearing when pictured leaving work at 6:36 p.m. on July 28. John Smith was found in a sofa on front of a TV. He sustained blunt force trauma to the top of his head, and received a stab wound to the neck, authorities said. As for their mother, she sustained blunt force trauma to the top of her head and received a stab wound to the neck. Authorities said she’d been dragged from a chair into John’s bedroom. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. results.title: Former Equifax CEO Before Senate Judiciary Panel - Part 1 : CSPAN3 : October 5, 2017 7:56am-9:03am EDT
results.description: Former Equifax CEO Richard Smith testified before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee on his former employer's response to a data breach that left more than 140 million consumers with their personal financial information at risk of theft. It was Mr. Smith's third such questioning in a week's time, and most of the subcommittee's inquiries focused on the speed of the credit reporting agency's response to the knowledge its data servers had been infiltrated by nefarious forces. The subcommittee took a break after Mr. Smith's testimony to vote on the Senate floor. Sponsor: Senate Judiciary Committee

results.title: Clusters in a cold climate : innovation dynamics in a diverse economy
results.creator: Innovation Systems Research Network. Conference (5th : 2003 : Ottawa, Ont.)
description: x, 228 pages : 24 cm

"As Canada emerges from the recent economic downturn, firms in industrial clusters face a series of unique challenges. From established clusters in auto parts and wine, to emerging clusters in biotechnology, photonics and multimedia, firms must adapt to rapidly changing demand and cost conditions, cope with increased competition at home and abroad, and finance an accelerating pace of innovation. The papers in this volume examine how firms in eight clusters are meeting these challenges by accessing resources and markets, managing economic uncertainty, and adapting to market changes. Representing the latest research findings from members of the Innovation Systems Research Network, the papers highlight a number of key themes: the contribution of both local and global sources of knowledge to innovation within the clusters, the powerful draw of external markets that can act as the primary stimulus to innovative behaviour, the interaction between key elements of the research infrastructure and innovative firms, and the complex, but essential, influence of public policy on cluster dynamics."--BOOK JACKET
Papers presented at the 5th Annual Conference of the Innovation Systems Research Network, held in Ottawa, Ont., May 1-2, 2003
Includes bibliographical references

Introduction: clusters in a cold climate / David A. Wolfe and Matthew Lucas -- Shifting gears: restructuring and innovation in the Ontario automotive parts industry / Susan Fitzgibbon [and others] -- Learning, innovation and cluster growth: a study of two inherited organizations in the Niagara Peninsula wine cluster / Lynn K. Mytelka and Haeli Goertzen -- Biotechnology companies and clustering in Nova Scotia / Philip Rosson and Carolan McLarney -- The biotechnology cluster in Vancouver / J. Adam Holbrook [and others] -- Networking and innovation in the Quebec optics/photonics cluster / Mélanie Kéroack, Mathieu Ouimet and Réjean Landry -- Clustered beginnings: anatomy of multimedia in Toronto / John N.H. Britton and Gerry Legare -- The Montreal multimedia sector: district, cluster or localized system of production? / Serge Rousseau -- Cluster or whirlwind? The new media industry in Vancouver / Richard Smith, Jane McCarthy and Michelle Petrusevich

results.title: Wilmington City Council Regular Meeting – March 4, 2025
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # Wilmington City Council Regular Meeting – March 4, 2025 The Wilmington City Council held its regular meeting on March 4, 2025, at 6:30 PM in City Hall. The meeting included presentations, public comments, public hearings, ordinances, resolutions, and a closed session. Key actions included approving a 5–2 rezoning for a commercial parking lot, unanimously supporting a substitute resolution urging NCDOT to explore all practical alternatives for the Cape Fear Memorial Bridge replacement, and accepting over $2.4 million in federal funding for a multi-use path. ### Presentations - Mayor Saffo read and presented a Proclamation naming March 2025 as Women’s History Month, accepted by Sheila Evans, Chair of the Wilmington/New Hanover County Commission for Women. - David Ingram (Sustainability Manager) and Richard Smith (Clean Energy Advisory Committee Chair) presented the annual report. Smith highlighted 2024 accomplishments: energy efficiency upgrades at police and fire headquarters (reducing energy usage intensity), LED retrofits, recommendations for a fleet EV transition study, adoption of a Sustainable Municipal Building Policy, and contributions to C-PACE. 2025 goals include expanding the EV pilot project (currently two Nissan Leafs at public works), pursuing SOLSMART Silver/Gold accreditation, and enhanced communication. Smith noted two current committee vacancies. ### Consent Calendar - **C1–C3** approved unanimously (7-0): - Approval of minutes from January 31, February 4, February 17, and February 18, 2025 council meetings. - Resolution authorizing a $332,347 golf cart lease agreement with Club Car, LLC for the Wilmington Municipal Golf Course. - Resolution authorizing retirement of Police Canine Officer Jacco and transfer to Corporal David Garriques. Mayor Saffo thanked K-9 Jacco for his service. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **Cynthia Gierer** (tenant at Arboretum West Apartments) described unresolved mold, pest, and plumbing issues after a pipe burst; she said code enforcement directed her to legal aid rather than taking action. - **Michael O’Leary** (resident in Brooklyn Arts District) opposed the social district pilot, citing noise, parking, public intoxication, and DUI risks. He provided statistics: North Carolina ranks third nationally in alcohol-related fatalities, with 345 fatal crashes and 12,146 alcohol-related crashes in 2023; estimated $10 billion annual cost of alcohol abuse in NC. He referenced a European study finding 19% of festival attendees drive home intoxicated. - **Alex White** (owner of Pizzeria Don Luca) supported the social district pilot, reporting that the three Saturdays of the program were the three busiest days in his shop’s history; sales doubled February 2024 totals, employee tips tripled, and he observed no negative incidents. He expressed willingness to address parking concerns. - **Elizabeth O’Donnell** (resident on South 2nd Street) urged council not to support a 135-foot fixed-span bridge, which she said would destroy her historic home and neighborhood. She supported the 100-foot option, noting reduced bridge openings (approximately 67 for sailboats in the past year) and lack of dredging plans north of the bridge. - **Elizabeth Wright** (resident on South 2nd Street) argued the 100-foot option is fiscally responsible and less disruptive. She cited declining large-vessel use north of the bridge, and warned that a 135-foot bridge could threaten federal funding and lead to tolls. She highlighted potential impacts to Davis Funeral Home and other historic businesses. - **Susan Bullock** (resident, Wrightsville Beach Chamber chair) requested postponement of the proposed U-5710 flyover bridge at Eastwood Road and Military Cutoff, suggesting the $85 million be reallocated. She described expected traffic congestion from overlapping construction projects. ### Public Hearings - **PH1 – Special Use Permit at 5651 Greenville Loop Road:** Unanimously continued (7-0) to June 17, 2025 meeting. - **PH2 – C-PACE Program:** Resolution authorizing City participation passed unanimously (7-0). David Ingram noted no budgetary impact and that New Hanover County adopted the program on February 17, 2025. - **PH3 – Rezoning at 4717 College Acres Drive** (R-5(CD) to CB(CD) for commercial parking lot): Staff recommended denial, citing inconsistency with the Comprehensive Plan; Planning Board recommended approval (5-2). After testimony from applicant Cindee Wolfe and property manager Grace Sneed (who presented 223 signatures in favor), council approved the rezoning on a 5-2 vote (Councilmembers Joyner and Andrews voted no). Second reading waived unanimously. - **PH4 – Rezoning at 5601 Oleander Drive** (CB to RB(CD) for commercial recreation center): Unanimously approved (7-0). Applicant John Reese described a 40,816 sq. ft. facility with arcade, bowling (10 lanes traditional, 8 duckpin), axe throwing, pickleball courts, restaurant, and bar. The applicant will install a traffic light at no cost to the city. Second reading waived. - **PH5 – Rezoning at 102 & 104 Meares Street** (R-3 to UMX): Unanimously approved (7-0). Applicant Christian Cardamone emphasized alignment with Southside Small Area Plan and potential for mixed-use infill. Second reading waived. - **PH6 – Rezoning at 6624 & 6710 Market Street** (R-15 to RB): Unanimously approved (7-0). Staff said the rezoning is consistent with surrounding commercial uses. Second reading waived. ### Discussion Items - **Clean Energy Advisory Committee Annual Report** (presented earlier). No separate discussion beyond presentation. - **Cape Fear Memorial Bridge Resolution:** Councilmember Andrews introduced a substitute resolution supporting a 100-foot fixed-span replacement. After extensive debate, the motion lacked a second. Mayor Saffo presented a substitute resolution urging NCDOT, US Coast Guard, and US Army Corps of Engineers to explore all practical alternatives to prevent negative impacts to homes, businesses, and historic structures. Councilmember Andrews moved, Mayor Saffo seconded; passed unanimously (7-0). Mayor Saffo noted that the state’s $242 million grant for the bridge could be at risk, and that any height determination may take up to five years of study. ### Key Outcomes - **Consent Calendar** approved 7-0. - **PH1** continued to June 17, 2025. - **PH2** (C-PACE) approved 7-0. - **PH3** (College Acres parking lot) approved 5-2; second reading waived 7-0. - **PH4** (Oleander Drive rec center) approved 7-0; second reading waived 7-0. - **PH5** (Meares Street rezoning) approved 7-0; second reading waived 7-0. - **PH6** (Market Street rezoning) approved 7-0; second reading waived 7-0. - **O1** (Gender equity grant) approved 7-0; second reading waived 7-0. - **O2a** (Energy block grant appropriation) approved 7-0; second reading waived 7-0. - **O2b** (Fleet EV transition strategy contract) approved 6-0 (one member absent). - **O3a** (South 17th Street MUP resolution) approved 6-0. - **O3b** (South 17th Street MUP appropriation) approved 6-0; second reading waived 7-0. - **Resolution on Cape Fear Memorial Bridge:** Substitute resolution (urging exploration of alternatives) passed 7-0; original resolution failed for lack of second. - Council entered closed session (6-0 vote) to discuss potential legal claims (Hunn v. City of Wilmington). No action taken; reconvened and adjourned at 9:35 PM.

results.title: North Kingstown Town Council Meeting Summary — June 22, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # North Kingstown Town Council Meeting — June 22, 2026 The North Kingstown Town Council held a regular meeting on Monday, June 22, 2026, at 7:00 PM in the Town Hall Council Chambers, 80 Boston Neck Road. The council is led by President Gregory A. Mancini, with members Linnea M. Drew, Elizabeth Hill Ross, Dr. Kimberly Ann Page, and Matthew B. McCoy. Notice of the meeting was posted on the Rhode Island Secretary of State's website pursuant to RIGL 42-46-6(c). The docket included special business on the Town Clerk appointment, a 19-item consent calendar (Items 7-25), the Town Manager's report, and new business covering numerous board appointments and a discussion of asphalt odor complaints in the West Davisville area. Record limitations: no meeting minutes were available, and the raw transcript contains no substantive discussion (only the word 'Okay'). As a result, no votes, motions, approvals, or outcomes can be confirmed from the available record. The timestamp associated with the record (2026-06-22 12:00:00 UTC) does not match the 7:00 PM start time listed on the agenda; this summary uses June 22, 2026 as the meeting date, consistent with the agenda. ### Special Business - Item 5: The Town Manager requested the Town Council's Advice and Consent for the appointment of Kerry Rollinson as Town Clerk. - Item 6: The Town Manager was scheduled to swear in Kerry Rollinson as Town Clerk following the council's action. ### Consent Calendar All items on the Consent Agenda (Items 7-25) were considered routine and were scheduled to be enacted by one motion, with items removed upon a request by a council member or citizen. - Item 7: Approval of minutes from the Special Meeting of March 30, 2026, and the Budget Public Hearings of April 13, 2026. - Item 8: Abatement of uncollectable taxes and fees totaling $128,692.57, including write-offs related to a deceased taxpayer and 2014 personal property, motor vehicle, and rescue accounts. - Item 9: Receipt of a donation of a hand-painted scoreboard to be painted on the side of the Field 1 storage shed at Ryan Park by Caitlin Wotherspoon. - Item 10: Award of contract to Envision Technology Advisors, LLC (State MPA #308) for an Information Technology Department Zero Trust True Up in the amount of $12,136.61, funded from the Granicus Video Streaming Software Account. - Item 11: Award of contract to Envision Technology Advisors (State MPA #308, Award #3806678) for Information Technology Managed Services Provider services in the amount of $156,600.00, funded from the FY2027 IT Maintenance Account. - Item 12: Award of a contract extension to CAI Technologies for Assessor's Parcel and Zoning Layer Maintenance and Web Geographic Information System Application, at various prices, funded from the Annual Miscellaneous Software License Account. - Item 13: Award of contract to BEI Holdings, dba Business Electronics, for one Detective Interview Room Recording System for the Police Department in the amount of $14,520.00, funded from the Police Capital Outlay Account. - Item 14: Approval of a sole source purchase from Motorola Solutions, Inc. of seven portable radios with accessories for the Police Department in the amount of $48,582.87 (State MPA #395), funded from the Police Capital Outlay Account. - Item 15: Award of a sole source purchase to Advanced Weighing Systems for an upgrade to the Department of Public Works Transfer Station scale computer software in the amount of $10,670.00, funded from the FY2026 Transfer Station Contractual Services Account. - Item 16: Approval of a purchase from Minuteman Security & Life Safety for Department of Senior Services security camera system upgrades and installation of an additional camera in the amount of $15,622.00 (State MPA #419), funded from the Capital Outlay Account. - Item 17: New entertainment license for Cocumscussoc Association, dba Smith's Castle, 55 Richard Smith Drive, for a live concert on the grounds of Smith's Castle on July 19, 2026 (rain date Sunday, August 2, 2026). - Item 18: New exhibition license (no vendors) for RI Elder Info, 70 Romano Vineyard Way, Suite 111, for the 7th Annual Calling All Veterans Day, a Veteran and Community Senior Resource Fair, on August 15, 2026 (rain date August 22, 2026). - Item 19: New fireworks permit for Plum Beach Club, 224 Plum Beach Road, Saunderstown, for a fireworks display on June 26, 2026 (rain date July 11, 2026). - Item 20: New fireworks permit for Quidnessett Country Club, 950 North Quidnessett Road, for a fireworks display on Tuesday, July 4, 2026, as stated in the agenda. - Item 21: Peddler license renewal for Keystone Novelties Distributors LLC to sell sparklers and novelty devices under a tent at 6653 Post Road. - Item 22: Peddler license renewal for Keystone Novelties Distributors LLC to sell sparklers and novelty devices under a tent at 4020 Quaker Lane. - Item 23: Victualling license renewal for Cloud Donuts, Inc., 6689 Post Road. - Item 24: Authorization for the Town Manager to sign and ratify a Memorandum of Understanding regarding the Town of North Kingstown's Remote Net Metering Agreement between the Town and the North Kingstown School Committee. - Item 25: First reading of an amendment to Section 2-1, entitled 'Competitive Bidding Required.' ### Public Comments & Testimony - The agenda provided a Public Comment period with a three-minute speaking limit, but no public testimony appears in the available transcript. ### Reports - Item 26: Report by the Town Manager, described in the agenda as including the Town Manager's regular update on Quonset-related issues. ### Discussion Items - Item 27: Asset Management Commission appointments: one School Committee Representative to July 1, 2029; one Technical Representative to July 1, 2029; three At-Large Representatives to July 1, 2029; and one At-Large Representative to July 1, 2027 to fill an unexpired term. Applications were attached from James Halley, Stephen Raymond, John Pyne, Lisa Bowe, and Andrew Sullivan. - Item 28: Building Code Board of Appeals: one member to July 1, 2031. - Item 29: Information Technology Advisory Committee: one Alternate At-Large Member to March 1, 2029. - Item 30: Leisure Services Advisory Committee: three members to July 1, 2029. Applications were attached from Keith Finck and Jeffrey Smith. - Item 31: Personnel Board: one member to March 1, 2029. - Item 32: Planning Commission: one member to July 1, 2032. An application was attached from Richard Lipsitz. - Item 33: Probate Judge to July 1, 2027. An application was attached from Brian Fielding. - Item 34: Veteran's Memorial Scholarship Fund Committee: two members to July 1, 2027. - Item 35: Wickford Village Design Guidelines Committee: one Alternate Business Property Owner to December 31, 2027. - Item 36: Councilor Beth Hill Ross requested discussion concerning Public Comment. - Item 37: Council President Mancini requested discussion and possible action regarding numerous complaints received by both the Town of North Kingstown and the Rhode Island Department of Environmental Management about the unacceptable asphalt smell in the West Davisville area. - Item 38: Correspondence. ### Key Outcomes - No decisions, votes, or actions can be confirmed from the available record. The raw transcript contains no substantive content, and no minutes were provided, so the council's disposition of the Town Clerk appointment, the consent calendar, the Town Manager's report, the appointments, or the asphalt odor discussion is not documented.

results.title: Donald Hartung Trial - Prosecution Closing Argument
results.creator: Law&Crime Network
results.description: NOTE: This is a Death Penalty Case. Donald Hartung, 63, stands trial in Escambia County, Florida for allegedly killing his mother Voncile Smith, 77, and his half-brothers John William Smith, 49, and Richard Thomas Smith, 47. He faces three counts of first-degree premeditated murder. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Escambia County deputies say the crimes happened July 28, 2015, according to an amended arrest report obtained by Law&Crime. Richard Smith, an employee of the Department of Homeland Security, had no-showed worked for a few days, so on deputies checked up on him on July 31. They found no sign of forced entry, but were able to enter through the back with the help of firefighters, and found the three victims dead throughout the home. Each person was under “large piles of clothes,” deputies said. Richard Smith had been shot around his right ear, and had a stab wound to the throat, deputies said. He was found face down in the TV room at the foot of the TV, investigators said. Authorities said he was wearing the same clothes he’d been wearing when pictured leaving work at 6:36 p.m. on July 28. John Smith was found in a sofa on front of a TV. He sustained blunt force trauma to the top of his head, and received a stab wound to the neck, authorities said. As for their mother, she sustained blunt force trauma to the top of her head and received a stab wound to the neck. Authorities said she’d been dragged from a chair into John’s bedroom. According to deputies, Hartung was at the house on the 28th to cook dinner, as usual. He left between 5:30 p.m. and 6:00 pm, he allegedly said, but he denied seeing his brother Richard. A neighbor, however, claimed to see Richard arrive at the residence before Hartung left, investigators said. This witness was not sure of the time, but said it was just before dark because the lights on Hartung’s car was not on, authorities said. Another witness–who was a co-worker’s of Hartung–said that he previously had a conversation with the defendant. In it, the alleged killer said that if anything happened to Voncile Smith, then he would inherit all of her property because he was the oldest son. The mom’s attorney, however, said that she’d kept him out of the will, deputies said. Hartung would’ve been the “potential sole heir” to his family’s estate because there were no other living relatives of the Smith family. The defendant has been called the “Blue Moon Killer” because at the time, the local sheriff described the slayings as “ritualistic” and apparently coincided with a semi-rare blue moon. results.description: Logbook kept by Josiah C. Long comprised of eight whaling voyages. First voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Shubael Chase, from 24 June 1822 - 27 December 1824 to the Pacific Ocean Contains a long description of the Bounty mutiny and people on Pitcairn Island. The crew also witnessed a total solar eclipse on 26 June 1824. Second voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Edy Coffin, from 7 June 1825 - 16 October 1827 to the Brazil banks, South Pacific Ocean and coast of ChileDuring this voyage the ship saw 125 whales and caught 97. During a stop at the Juan Fernández Islands the ship was able to obtain peaches for the ship. There was one death at sea. Third voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Job C. Clark, from 19 April 1828 - 30 June 1829 to western and southern Atlantic Ocean for sperm and right whales [spelled "write"]. Fourth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Job E. Clark, from 15 November 1829 - 27 January 1833 to the Atlantic Ocean and Pacific Ocean sIn the company of several other vessel at times. Put into port at Rio de Janeiro for repairs. Fifth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 27 June 1833 - 16 November 1836 along Brazil and Chile and the South Pacific OceanDuring the voyage they saw 86 whales and caught 52. They spoke the Charles Carroll's captain Owen Chase who was a survivor of the Essex. Sixth voyage documents the Foster (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 1 September 1837 - 28 April 1841 to waters off Brazil, Chile, Peru and the South Pacific OceanThe ship encountered rough weather and could not reach the Azores. During the voyage nine men contracted smallpox. Seveth voyage documents the Richard Mitchell (Ship) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 14 October 1843 - 30 September 1847 to Brazil, Galapagos Islands, and the South Pacific OceanIncludes comments on the residents of Pitcairn Islands. It took the ship a month to round Cape Horn. Eighth voyage documents the Charles Carroll (Ship : 1832-1853) of Nantucket, Mass., mastered by Josiah C. Long, from 2 December 1848 - 29 December 1852 along the coast of Peru and the South Pacific Ocean. Voyage began by wrecking the rudder on an oil cask. results.creator: René Viénet
results.description: Roch Marcandier HISTOIRE DES HOMMES DE PROYE ou Les Crimes du Comité de Surveillance et des buveurs de sang, dénoncés à tous les peuples.  Il subsiste peu d’ exemplaires originaux de ce pamphlet : selon WorldCat, à la bibliothèque de la Fondation Thiers à Paris et un autre à la BNF. Egalement à la British Library, la National Library of Scotland, Roger Williams U. Library,  U. of  Leeds Library.  En ligne, sous   Internet Archive , un scan complet  - l'exemplaire de la Newberrys - est disponible : https://archive.org/details/histoiredeshomme00marc/page/3/mode/1up La présente édition en ligne reprend, en caractère Didot, l'originale de 1792 de Roch Marcandier (66 pages, Imprimerie des Droits de l'Homme) de notre exemplaire original, acheté chez un libraire parisien.  L'orthographe et la ponctuation en ont été respectées, en intégrant dans le corps du texte [signalées entre crochets, en caractère maigre] les notes en bas de page de l'auteur.   La pagination de cette version mise en ligne est aberrante compte-tenu d’un certain nombre de pages à venir dans l’édition  libraire. Le texte original diffère légèrement de la réédition en 1835 par Buchez & Roux dans le 18e tome (page 181 à 215) de leur " Histoire parlementaire de la Révolution française ... " (40 volumes, Paris, Paulin, 1834-1838).  Le fichier photographique de notre exemplaire original, plus clair que celui de la Newberrys, sera également mis en ligne - sur ce même site Internet Archive - en attendant une édition définitive libraire, avec notre introduction mise à jour. Dans cette introduction, dont une première version est mise en ligne séparément sous   Internet Archive , il est expliqué pourquoi  certains § sont surlignés en jaune  : il s’agît des passages que L-S. Mercier —  dans son  Nouveau Paris —  a dérobé à Marcandier,  sans jamais le citer, ni même mentionner son exécution. Bien évidemment, aucun des spécialistes de Mercier ne s’en est aperçu, ni malheureusement aucun des spécialistes (plus rares) de Roch Marcandier  … Ces  trois mises en ligne (la numérisation de l’édition originale, sa reprise en typographie, notre introduction provisoire) sont réalisées en octobre 2021, à l’occasion d’un débat sur Marie-Olympe de Gouges,  et les Massacres de septembre. René Viénet

results.title: 449 Stealing America: Indigenous Slavery and the American Revolution
results.creator: YORK UNITED METHODIST CHURCH
results.description: More than half a million Indigenous people were enslaved within the present-day borders of the United States. Historian Linford Fisher spent fifteen years in archives across North America, the Caribbean, and Britain to investigate this forgotten history. What he found was not a second story running alongside African slavery. It was something different in kind. Europeans and early Americans enslaved people who lived on land they intended to possess. This practice made slavery a tool of dispossession. The American Revolution is where this process accelerated. Lin and Lorén Spears, a Narragansett tribal citizen and the executive director of the Tomaquag Museum , trace how the Revolution opened space for captive raiding on the western frontier, how Native nations weighed which side to take during the war, and how their Stolen Relations digital project is recovering the names of the Natives early Americans enslaved. "Reissued in response to demand, this definitive anthology of colonial American poetry is made available in a classroom edition, with annotatory emendations reflecting recent scholarship. The book presents 250 representative poems—fifty-nine printed here for the first time—accompanied by Professor Meserole's illuminating introduction, notes, glosses, comments, and catalogue of sources.The poets represented range from well-known writers such as Anne Bradstreet, Edward Taylor, and Michael Wigglesworth to personages not known primarily for their poetry—including Cotton Mather, Governor William Bradford, Roger Williams, and Captain John Smith—to the less famous such as schoolteacher Sarah Kemble Knight, lawyer Richard Chamberlain, and former indentured servant George Alsop. The poetry here offers a wide range of expression, including love lyrics, religious meditation, political satire, elegies, and personal narratives." --Publisher's Description

John Murrill, professor pf history, likes to say that the Federal Constitutional Convention held 200 years ago in Philadelphia was the first Princeton alumni college. Of the 55 delegates who composed the Constitution between May and September of 1787, nine were Princeton alumni; this was nearly twice as many as from any other American or Britjsh college. Princetonians, Murrin poilts out, led each of the three factions that dominated the convention. James Madison, Class of 1771, pushed the Virginia Plan, and William Paterson, Class of 1763, presented and vigorously defended the New Jersey Plan, which appealed to the small states. Neither of these models for the Constitution was ultimately adopted.' But among the leaders who promoted the plan that was adopted-a lower house elected in proportion to population and an upper house in which each state, regardless of size had equal representation-Oliver Ellsworth of Connecticut, a member of the Class of 1766, figured prominently. One of the tensest moments at the convention was provided by Gunning Bedford Jr. of Delaware, valedictorian of the Class of 1771. During the deliberations, Bedford declared, "The large states dare not dissolve the confederation. If they do the small ones -will find some-foreign ally of more honor and good faith, who will take them by the hand and do them justice." "He did not mean by this to intimidate.' or ' alarm," wrote James Although Bedford later apologized, "his speech sobered everyone," according to Murrin. Of the 55 delegates to the convention, 25-including George Washington and Benjamin. Franklin-had not attended any college. Five had attended William and Mary, and the same number had been to Yale. Three were Harvard graduates and three Columbia. Two had been to the University of Pennsylvania, one to Oxford and one to Glasgow. I ' (One delegate had studied at three. Scottish universities.) The Princetonian delegates represented six different states, while the Yale men came from four, and all the Harvard graduates were from Massachusetts. The other Princeton "alumni present were Alexander Martin,, Class of 1756, of North Carolina; Luther Mart; 1766, Maryland; William C. Houston, 1768, New Jersey (he had been a professor of mathematics and natural philosophy at Princeton); William R. Davie, 1776, z North Carolina; and Jonathan Davie, 1776, New Jersey. results.title: 449 Stealing America: Indigenous Slavery and the American Revolution
results.creator: YORK UNITED METHODIST CHURCH
results.description: More than half a million Indigenous people were enslaved within the present-day borders of the United States. Historian Linford Fisher spent fifteen years in archives across North America, the Caribbean, and Britain to investigate this forgotten history. What he found was not a second story running alongside African slavery. It was something different in kind. Europeans and early Americans enslaved people who lived on land they intended to possess. This practice made slavery a tool of dispossession. The American Revolution is where this process accelerated. Lin and Lorén Spears, a Narragansett tribal citizen and the executive director of the Tomaquag Museum , trace how the Revolution opened space for captive raiding on the western frontier, how Native nations weighed which side to take during the war, and how their Stolen Relations digital project is recovering the names of the Natives early Americans enslaved. Sharply observed and metaphorically inventive, Ocean Effects is a worthy follow-up to Galvin's National Book Award finalist Habitat. It includes a new vein of Galvin's trademark richly observed lyric poems on the biota, landscapes, and weathers of coastal New England. Seascapes and the natural world bracket sequences spoken by personae as various as the seventeenth-century American colonist Roger Williams, small-town cops, a squatter in the ruins of Chernobyl, a nineteenth-century Russian general in Mongolia, and a Cape Cod carpenter. results.title: Cranston City Council Budget Hearing for FY2026-2027 - April 16, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # Cranston City Council Finance Committee Budget Hearing - April 16, 2026 The Cranston City Council Finance Committee held a public hearing on the proposed FY2026-2027 budget on April 16, 2026, starting at approximately 7:39 PM and adjourning at 11:49 PM. The meeting focused on the mayor's proposed 7.44% tax levy increase and the financial challenges facing the city, particularly the school department. The committee heard testimony from school committee members, citizens, and representatives from police, fire, schools, and other departments. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **School Committee Vice Chair Anthony Melillo** (33 Harvard Street) presented "myths vs facts," stating that Cranston Public Schools reduced staff by 95 positions over the past four years (not added 100), and that over the last six years the city allocation increased by only about $1 million annually on average, which has not kept pace with rising costs. He emphasized shared responsibility for the budget challenges. - **School Committee Member Catherine Crowley** (Ward 6) explained the school department's structural deficit, noting that the mayor's proposed $1.5 million increase is insufficient. She warned that cuts would lower education quality and deter new teachers. - **School Committee Member Keith Catone** (61 Windsor Road) challenged claims of deficits, stating the school department only recorded a deficit in FY25, while FY24, 23, and 22 had surpluses. He argued that the city budget has been balanced "on the backs of the schools" and that transparency is needed to build public trust. - **Resident Valerie (last name unclear)** stated that taxpayers have "nothing left to give" and urged the council to find budget cuts rather than increase taxes, emphasizing the strain on seniors and families. - **Councilman Steven Steikos** (37 Ferncrest Avenue) observed that school funding increased only 4.3% total from 2024 to 2027, while fire and police funding increased 15.6% and 12.5% respectively. He also noted an $852,000 cash balance in the charter school account and suggested reviewing tax breaks for veterans and elderly. - **Resident Stephen Fryers** (107 Garden Hills Drive) said the budget problem is a "failure in local government" due to over-reliance on one-time federal ARPA funds. He recommended spending cuts and not going above an 8% tax rate effect. - **School Committee Member Anna Madeiris** (21 Bridgeton Court) shared positive stories of student achievements and urged full funding for schools, warning that deteriorating buildings and large class sizes hurt students. - **School Committee Chair Dominic Fusco** (no address provided) noted that Cranston spends $19,950 per student, well below the state average of $22,800. He said the school department has "no choice now but to close schools, increase class sizes, cut programs." - **Local 1363 President Jonathan Francis** (35 Fifth Avenue) defended the fire department, stating that a fifth rescue was added after 40 years and that the department faces 12 vacancies. He said minimum manning of 43 firefighters per shift falls short of the national standard. - **Seventh grader Sally Finkel** (55 Roger Williams Circle) asked to fully fund schools to preserve middle school sports, which she said give students motivation and community. ### Discussion Items #### Police Department Budget (Chief Winquist, Director Strom) - Proposed budget: $33 million. The chief described the budget as "bare bones" and stated that overtime budget of $2.2 million is aligned with historical averages. There are six vacancies; the department had to reduce vehicle purchases from eight to six due to cuts. - Revenue projections were adjusted downward because previous years were overestimated (e.g., police detail car revenues were underperforming). - The department is in contract negotiations; a contingency line item of $700,000 is included for potential contract costs. - Council members questioned gas/oil budget adequacy ($12,500 increase) and the need for more police vehicles given high mileage. The acting director noted oil prices are speculative but assumed the Middle East conflict would not persist. #### Animal Control (Chief Winquist) - The shelter is handling more animals due to economic pressures; budget increase of $10,000 for care. Revenue from impound fees is projected lower due to conservative estimates. - The department uses social media to promote adoptions; average stay is 4-6 weeks. #### Harbor Master - No current harbor master since previous one passed away. The city still collects mooring fees (~$3,500 last year without a harbor master). The council discussed whether to reinstate the position (stipend $3,500) or have police handle duties, but noted the net revenue gain is small. #### School Department Budget (Superintendent Massey, CFO Balducci) - The school department requested $4.2 million new city funding to meet contractual obligations (salary and benefits). The mayor proposed $1.5 million. The state aid increase is estimated at $2 million, but when accounting for a $241,000 reduction in non-public transportation support, net new state money is about $1.8 million. - The school department has a budget savings gap of approximately $3 million (assumes $4 million city ask). If only $1.5 million is provided, the gap grows to $2.5 million. - Cranston Public Schools has cut 95 staff over the last six years and laid off 40 teachers this year; about 12 will likely not be called back. Class sizes are already at contractual limits, and further cuts will increase class sizes and reduce services. - The district spends $19,950 per student, well below the state average. Inflation since 2009 is 56-58%, but city funding only increased 18% over the same period. - Health insurance costs have risen 15% and 10% in the last two years; the district is self-insured and part of a collaborative. A cumulative deficit of $9 million exists, but a new pharmacy contract is expected to generate $4.5 million annually to reduce it. - Charter school impact: $7.2 million in FY25 in tuition and lost state aid. - Discussion of selling former school buildings (Barrows, Waterman) to generate $750,000 one-time for capital needs, but that will not be available in future years. The city solicitor clarified the funds are intended for capital improvements, not tuition. #### Fire Department Budget (Chief, Director Strom) - Proposed overtime budget: $6.3 million (up slightly from FY25 actual of $6.073 million). The chief noted summer overtime is highest and 12 firefighters short, with vacancies due to contractual limits. Fuel costs are a concern due to global prices. - There are 15 firefighters on occupational injury; seven are waiting for state pension board decisions. These injuries increase overtime. - The department had to cut vehicle replacements; two staff vehicles are included. - Council members expressed concern about accuracy of overtime projections given prior years' underfunding. #### Fire Alarm Department - Budget increased for computer maintenance and repairs (licenses increasing). No significant questions. #### Canvassing Department (Director Lima via video) - Proposed operating budget for elections: $215,000, the lowest since 2018. Savings achieved by reducing poll workers (from 315 to 270), cutting poll worker management software (delayed until federal funds available), and benefits from moving the primary to Wednesday (saving ~$25,000). - The department faces increased voter registration transactions (23,822 in 2025) and security needs. Federal election security grant ($50,000) has been fully spent on physical security upgrades. - Potential new state Voting Rights Act may require bilingual ballots, increasing costs. Director Lima noted that federal executive orders could impact mail ballot processing. #### Law Department (Solicitor) - Running under budget at 72.8% year-to-date. No provision for lawsuit settlements; the solicitor recommended budgeting a small contingency. Outside legal services are used for specialized cases and are negotiated at municipal rates (~$200/hour). #### Executive Office (Director Moretti) - Proposing a 0.75% increase (less than 1%), achieved by eliminating one administrative position and consolidating government affairs with communications. Compensation increases for 18 administrative appointees (totaling ~$45,000) were included, but the mayor offered to forego those raises if the council desires, reallocating funds to police vehicles. - The mayor receives a $3,000 annual expense stipend (not monthly). Four city vehicles are assigned to executive staff; fuel and maintenance are charged to the police budget—a legacy accounting practice. Council members questioned this and requested transparency. ### Key Outcomes - No final votes on the budget were taken. The committee will continue deliberations in subsequent hearings, including a planned executive session regarding police contract negotiations. - The council president noted that a 7.44% tax levy increase would require seven out of nine votes (four-fifths) per the city charter, and that nothing is finalized. - The council extended the meeting twice by 30-minute increments to allow full discussion. - Public comment was invited at the meeting's start and end; no online participants spoke. - The meeting adjourned at 11:49 PM.

results.title: Indian giving : economies of power in Indian-white exchanges
results.creator: Murray, David, 1945-
description: viii, 258 pages ; 24 cm

"In this book, David Murray explores a range of early exchanges between Europeans and Indians, showing how they operated within a set of interlocking economies - linguistic, religious, as well as material." "To illustrate the complexities of these cross-cultural transactions, the author looks closely at the work of linguist, trader, and missionary Roger Williams, whose A Key into the Language of America at once serves the purposes of translation, conversion, and trade. Murray also examines the changing meaning and representation of wampum, the quintessential medium of exchange in the early colonial period, as well as the multiple processes of conversion taking place as Christian ideas were incorporated into Indian cultures."--Jacket
Includes bibliographical references (pages 233-249) and index

results.title: Indian & English dictionary
creator: Swan, Bradford F. (Bradford Fuller) fmo RIBRL
Rhode Island Historical Society. Library. fmo RIBRL
description: Ms. codex
Title taken from ms. slip of covers of volumes 1-3
Dates of publication suggested by JCB Catalogue of manuscript codices

Originally made up of eight volumes, this manuscript Indian and English dictionary consists of four surviving volumes. Based on an extensive compilation process in which terms for various North American Indian languages were collected from different sources. The sources used included A key into the language of America / by Roger Williams, first printed in 1643, with words in the Narragansett language, designated as "RW" in the manuscript, a list of Nanticoke terms labeled as "Nan" and other lists as yet unidentified, labeled as "A", "B", "C", "H", "L", "S", "W", and "Z"

Dictionary entries were written on lined paper and then cut out as individual slips and pasted onto the pages of unrelated printed books in an alphabetical arrangement, forming an attempt at a comprehensive dictionary of Indian and English terms, probably limited to Algonquian languages used in the northeastern United States

Volume 1 has 142 pages and consists of entries Aa to Me; the papers are pasted on the sheets of volume 2 of The history of the wars which arose out of the French Revolution to which is prefixed, a review of the causes of that event / by Alexander Stephens, Philadelphia, 1804. This volume retains its title page, is bound in full contemporary mottled calf and measures 22 cm. tall

Volume 2 has p. 171-359 and consists of entries Me to Wa; the papers are pasted on sheets made up from a German hymnbook. This volume is bound in contemporary full mottled calf and measures 18 cm. tall

Volume 3 has p. 360-421 and consists of entries Wa to Zed, and a supplementary list for entried Ach to Yu, on p. 422-447; the papers are pasted on sheets made up from a German theological text. This volume is bound in contemprary full mottled calf and measures 17 cm. tall
Volumes 1-3 are housed in three cream cloth covered phase boxes with volumes 3 and 4 being housed together; the phase boxes measure 25 cm. tall
John Carter Brown Library copy acquired from the estate of Bradford F. Swan

results.title: East Providence City Council Meeting - July 7, 2026
results.creator: OpenPublica
results.description: # East Providence City Council Meeting - July 7, 2026 This regular meeting of the East Providence City Council covered a range of topics including sewer abatements, proclamations, a public hearing and final passage of an ordinance appropriating $340,035 for softball field improvements, approvals of licenses, communications from the SBA, and various council member items regarding infrastructure, public safety, and community events. The meeting concluded with several resolutions and adjournment. ### Consent Calendar - **Sewer Charge Abatement:** Approved $378.58 abatement for a water break related to a bathroom pipe, recommended by the Department of Public Works. Motion by Councilman Bogarty, seconded by Councilman Lawson. Unanimous. - **Consent Calendar Items:** Council journals (June 16, 2026), new addresses (156 Amarillo St, 9 Regent Drive), cancellations and abatements ($6,647.24). Motion by Councilwoman Sousa, seconded by Councilman Fogerty. Unanimous. - **Licenses:** Bundled items 1-10 (entertainment, alcohol, new business licenses for East Providence Fuel, etc.) approved with a motion by Councilman Lawson and second by Councilwoman Sousa. Unanimous. ### Public Comments & Testimony - **Softball Field Improvements (Public Hearing):** Multiple speakers expressed support for lighting and improvements at Amaral Field. - Richard Hogan (President of East Providence Central Little League) detailed the league's growth (200-250 players, 80 volunteers), the lack of lights causing scheduling difficulties, and the need for equity with baseball fields. He noted that the junior/senior division girls will represent Rhode Island in Pennsylvania. - Christina O'Reilly (coach and parent) explained that without lights, older girls (13-15) cannot practice after school, limiting seasons. She cited a Women's Sports Foundation study that girls drop out at twice the rate of boys by age 14. - Jonathan McGowan (Vice President of East Providence Central Little League) highlighted the growth from 76 players to nearly 100 in one year and urged support. - A resident (parent of six, five girls) spoke in favor, showing the growth in divisions (coach pitch, minors, majors, juniors/seniors) and the team's success in all-stars. - **Additional Hours for Fuel Sales (Public Hearing):** No public speakers for or against. The applicant (Nicholas Lambrose, attorney) explained the need for 24-hour fuel sales at the new East Providence Fuels (formerly Exxon). The council clarified that during 1 a.m. to 6 a.m., only fuel sales would occur, not repairs. Approved with that condition. ### Discussion Items - **Council President Rodrigues - World Cup Recognition:** Rodrigues thanked the Scottish "Tartan Army" for their positive impact, including a $10,000 donation to Hasbro Children's Hospital and general goodwill. He wore a kilt in tribute. - **Councilman Lawson - Budget Requests:** Proposed adding a DPW rodent/pest control specialist (like Cranston and Warwick), improvements to Oldham (city-owned building), and reviewing school department head teaching loads. The administration acknowledged and will consider. - **Councilman Lawson - Parking for Crescent Park Events:** With construction reducing parking, he suggested shuttles from off-site lots, local traffic restrictions, and using private lots. Councilwoman Sousa noted that a shuttle was used for the recent block party and should be replicated. The administration will coordinate. - **Councilman Lawson - Willet Avenue Traffic Redesign:** He criticized the road diet and yield sign configuration, stating residents feel ignored. Administration explained the redesign was based on resident feedback and engineering standards to reduce speeding, with no major accidents reported. Lawson disagreed, calling the road diet unsafe. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Veterans Hero Banners:** Out of 108 orders, 86 paid; banners have been ordered and will be installed by August on Roger Williams Ave, Bullocks Point Ave, and Pawtucket Ave (pending confirmation). A digital payment option will be implemented for future orders. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Pedestrian Crosswalks on Warren Avenue:** Asked for timeline on crosswalk signals at Lions Ave and 7th St. Administration will check with DPW director Dan. Sousa stressed safety issues for children crossing to bus stops. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Speed Monitoring on Burgess Avenue:** Requested traffic study and calming measures. Council Vice President Rigo recommended contacting police chief for a traffic study first. Administration will request study from chief. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Street Light Adjustment:** Requested brighter lighting in dark neighborhoods, especially near parks. Administration noted balance between safety, energy cost, and bulb life, and will review specific locations. - **Councilwoman Sousa - Trash Receptacles at Parks and Bus Stops:** Requested more trash cans at parks (e.g., Martello Park) and bus stops. Administration stated RIPTA is responsible for bus stops, but will coordinate; they noted a carry-in/carry-out policy and capacity limits for 44 parks. - **Council Vice President Rigo - ADU Tax Stabilization:** Second passage of ordinance amending tax stabilization for qualified businesses to include accessory dwelling units (ADUs), for owner-occupied properties with homestead exemption only. Rigo explained it helps with housing crisis without building on new land. Passed 4-1. - **Resolutions:** - **Window Replacement at City Hall:** Contract with Red Oak Remodeling for $482,545 for exterior windows, previously discussed. Unanimous. - **Easement for Police Substation:** Granting easement to Narragansett Electric for power to police substation at Pierce Field, previously discussed. Unanimous. - **Furniture for Community Center:** Authorizing purchase of furniture, fixtures, and equipment from W.B. Mason for $172,539.75, using previously allocated funds (ARPA/CPF grant). Unanimous. ### Key Outcomes - **Sewer Abatement Approved** Unanimous. - **Consent Calendar and Licenses Approved** Unanimous. - **Pierce Softball Field Improvements Ordinance Approved** Unanimously (second passage, public hearing held). The $340,035 allocation covers lights, paved parking, walkways, guardrails, and will be contracted with New School Lighting. - **Additional Hours for Fuel Sales Approved** (with condition of no repairs between 1 a.m. and 6 a.m.) Unanimous. - **ADU Tax Stabilization Ordinance Approved** 4-1. - **Resolutions for City Hall Windows, Easement, and Community Center Furniture Approved** Unanimously. - **Veterans Hero Banners:** Expected installation by August. - **Willet Avenue Traffic Pattern:** Administration stands by redesign; further complaints will be brought back. - **Various Council Requests:** Administration will follow up on parking, speed monitoring, crosswalks, street lights, and trash receptacles.
